lessons.title: The Musical Alphabet and the Octave
body: Western music uses seven natural note names: A, B, C, D, E, F, G. After G the pattern starts again, but at a higher pitch, and the distance from one letter to its next appearance is called an octave. The two notes sound like the same note at different heights, which is why they share a name.

On a piano the pattern is easy to see. Middle C is the C nearest the middle of a standard keyboard, and moving to the right makes the pitch higher. A full piano has 88 keys and runs from A0 to C8, a range wider than any other common acoustic instrument. The number after each letter in this scientific pitch notation tells you which octave it belongs to, so C4 is middle C and C5 is the next C up.

Instruments are described by this same system. A violin goes from about G3 to A7, a cello from C2 to C6, and the double bass reaches down to E1. Reading these ranges is the first step in understanding what each instrument can do.
A simple example is singing the first line of a song and then repeating it an octave higher: the tune is the same but sits higher.

lessons.title: Sharps, Flats and the Twelve Tones
body: The smallest step in Western music is the semitone, also called the half step. On a piano it is the distance from a key to the very next key, black or white. A sharp raises a note by one semitone and a flat lowers it by one. So C-sharp is the black key just above C, and D-flat is the same key named from the other side. Two names for one pitch are called enharmonic equivalents.

There is a black key between most pairs of natural notes, but not between E and F or between B and C, where the white keys are already one semitone apart. Counting every key from one C to the next C gives twelve different pitches, which is why this is called the twelve-tone system. Thirteen notes appear if you include both Cs, but the top C is the start of the next octave.
The name used depends on context. A composer writing in a key full of flats will call the note D-flat, while one in a key of sharps will write C-sharp.
Playing up a piano one key at a time, you are climbing in semitones.

lessons.title: The Staff and Clefs
body: Music is written on a staff, a set of five horizontal lines with four spaces between them. A note sits either on a line or in a space, and the higher it sits on the staff, the higher the pitch. When a melody goes beyond the staff, small extra lines called ledger lines extend it.

A staff on its own does not say which pitches the lines mean. A clef symbol at the start does that. The treble clef is used for higher-pitched instruments and voices, such as the violin, flute and soprano. The bass clef is used for lower instruments such as the cello, bassoon and tuba. The viola is read in the alto clef, a clef that places middle C on the middle line and suits an instrument whose range sits between the violin and the cello.
Many instruments are written in one clef, while the piano uses two staves joined together, with the treble clef for the right hand and the bass clef for the left.
If you look at a piece for choir you may see the same logic: sopranos and altos on a treble staff, tenors and basses lower down.

lessons.title: Rhythm: Note Values and Rests
body: Every written note has a duration. A whole note lasts four beats, a half note two beats, a quarter note one beat and an eighth note half a beat. These values are relative, not absolute. The tempo, or speed, decides how long a beat lasts in real time.

Tempo is often given in beats per minute. At 120 beats per minute there are two beats every second, so one beat lasts half a second. A half note at that speed lasts one second, and a whole note lasts two seconds. If the tempo slows to 60 beats per minute, the same quarter note lasts a full second, though it is still one beat on the page.

Silence matters as much as sound. Every note value has a matching rest, so a quarter rest is one beat of silence. Learning to feel rests, not just fill them, is one of the first marks of a developing musician.
A drummer counting "one, two, three, four" is counting quarter-note beats, and the hi-hat playing between the counts is playing eighth notes.

lessons.title: Meter and Time Signatures
body: Beats are grouped into measures, also called bars, and the time signature at the start of a piece says how. In the time signature, the top number says how many beats are in each measure, and the bottom number says which note value counts as one beat. So 4/4 means four quarter-note beats per measure. It is the most common signature in popular music.

A 3/4 signature gives three beats and the lilt of a waltz. A 6/8 signature has six eighth notes per measure grouped in two sets of three, which creates a rolling compound rhythm. The grouping matters more than the total: 6/8 sounds like two big beats, each divided in three, rather than six equal pulses.
The strongest beat of a measure is beat one, and many styles accent other beats too. In rock the snare drum typically lands on the backbeat, beats two and four of a 4/4 measure.

A measure of 4/4 can be filled by a half note and two quarter notes, since 2 + 1 + 1 equals 4. Beethoven's fifth symphony is built from a short-short-short-long rhythmic motif, which shows how a tiny rhythm can generate a whole movement.

lessons.title: The Major Scale and Keys
body: A scale is an ordered sequence of notes. The major scale follows a pattern of whole steps (W) and half steps (H): W-W-H-W-W-W-H. A whole step is two semitones and a half step is one. Add them up and 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 equals 12 semitones, which is exactly one octave.

Starting on C, the pattern gives C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C, all the white keys of a piano. That is why C major is the easiest key to learn. Starting on G, the same pattern gives G-A-B-C-D-E-F#-G. The F-sharp is needed because the step from E up to the seventh note must be a whole step, so that the last step to G is a half step.

Every major key has its own set of sharps or flats, called its key signature, and there are twelve major keys in total. When a composer says a piece is in C major, almost all of the notes come from that scale. The first note of the scale, the tonic, feels like home, while other notes feel tense and want to move.
Singing do-re-mi is singing a major scale.

lessons.title: Intervals: Measuring the Distance
body: An interval is the distance between two pitches. It has a number name, found by counting the letter names spanned, and a quality such as perfect, major, minor, augmented or diminished. From C up to G you pass C, D, E, F, G, which is five letter names, so the interval is a fifth.

Some intervals are called perfect: the unison, fourth, fifth and octave. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are major or minor. A major third, such as C to E, spans four semitones. A minor third, such as C to E-flat, spans three. That single semitone is the difference between a major chord and a minor chord.

Musicians learn to hear intervals through familiar tunes. The opening of Twinkle, Twinkle is a perfect fifth, and the first two notes of Here Comes the Bride are a perfect fourth. Do-Re-Mi begins with a major second.
A practical check: C to A spans C, D, E, F, G, A, six letter names, so it is a sixth. Ear training means recognising these distances instantly, without counting.

lessons.title: Ratios: The Octave 2:1 and the Fifth 3:2
body: Pitch depends on the frequency of a vibration, counted in hertz (Hz), the number of cycles per second. The standard tuning note A4 is 440 Hz. The octave has the simplest ratio of all: the higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast, a ratio of 2:1. So the A an octave above 440 Hz is 880 Hz, and the A an octave below is 220 Hz. This is why two notes an octave apart sound like the same note.

The perfect fifth has the next simplest ratio, 3:2. Multiply by 3/2 to find the fifth above a note, so the fifth above 440 Hz is 660 Hz. Violin strings are tuned in fifths, G-D-A-E, and each string is a 3:2 ratio from the one below.

Brass instruments show the same idea. Before valves, a trumpet could only play notes in the harmonic series of its tubing, whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of a base. High in the series the harmonics lie close enough to form a scale, so Baroque trumpet parts live very high.
Simple ratios are the reason these intervals sound so stable.

lessons.title: Triads: Stacking Thirds
body: A chord is several notes sounding together, and the basic chord is the triad: three notes stacked in thirds. A major triad is built from a root, a major third above it and a perfect fifth above it. On C that spells C-E-G. In semitones the thirds are 4 and then 3, which adds up to 7 from the root to the fifth.

A minor triad uses a minor third in place of the major one, so C minor is C-E-flat-G. A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds: root, minor third and diminished fifth, such as C-E-flat-G-flat. An augmented triad stacks two major thirds. Major, minor, diminished and augmented are the four triad qualities, and they are the building blocks of harmony.
To build any major triad, find the root, count four semitones up for the third and seven for the fifth. On G this gives G-B-D.
If you strum an open guitar chord, you are hearing a triad, perhaps with some notes doubled in other octaves.

lessons.title: Chord Function and Seventh Chords
body: In any key, chords built on different scale degrees have different jobs. The I chord, the tonic, is home and rest. The V chord, the dominant, creates tension and wants to resolve back to I. The IV chord, the subdominant, provides contrast. In the key of C major these chords have roots C, F and G. These three chords, I, IV and V, underpin the blues, rock, country, gospel and classical music alike.

Add a fourth note, another third above the fifth, and a triad becomes a seventh chord. The dominant seventh, V7, is especially strong. In C major, G7 is G-B-D-F, and the added F sharpens the pull toward C. Jazz harmony is built on stacked sevenths, then ninths, elevenths and thirteenths.

Harmony is not always played all at once. In Bach's cello suites, one line implies four-part harmony. If you follow only the bass notes you can hear a complete chord progression that is never actually played. Pachelbel's Canon repeats a two-bar ground bass twenty-eight times while the voices move above it.
In a pop song the verse usually sits on I and IV, and V returns to home.

lessons.title: Modes: Other Colours of the Scale
body: Medieval church music organised pitch in seven modes. Each mode is a rotation of the major scale, starting from a different degree. The first mode, Ionian, is the major scale itself. Dorian starts on the second degree and sounds like a minor scale with a raised sixth. Phrygian starts on the third degree and has a Spanish flavour. Lydian, on the fourth, is dreamy because of its raised fourth. Mixolydian, on the fifth, is a major scale with a flattened seventh, often called the rock scale. Aeolian, on the sixth, is the natural minor, and Locrian, on the seventh, is diminished and rarely used.
The white keys give an easy demonstration. Playing the white keys from D to D gives Dorian, from A to A gives Aeolian, and from G to G gives Mixolydian.

In modal music the focus shifts away from the dominant pull. A piece may stay on one sustained sound or chord, which gives a static, meditative quality; Gregorian chant gets a similar feel from a single unaccompanied melody. Miles Davis explored Dorian and Mixolydian in Kind of Blue in 1959, and Mixolydian colours many rock songs, where the flattened seventh gives a bluesy lift.

lessons.title: Instrument Families and How They Sound
body: Instruments are grouped into families by how they produce sound. In the strings, a stretched string is set vibrating by a bow, a finger or a hammer, and a hollow body amplifies it. In the woodwinds, a column of air inside a tube is set vibrating by an edge, a single reed or a double reed, and opening holes changes its length. The flute has no reed: the player splits an airstream against an edge. The oboe uses a double reed, two cane blades vibrating against each other.

In brass, the buzzing of the player's lips is the vibrating source, and valves or a slide change the length of tubing to select a different harmonic series. In percussion, a membrane, bar, plate or body is struck and allowed to ring. Timpani and marimba have definite pitch, while the snare drum and cymbals have indefinite pitch.

A keyboard is an interface rather than a sound source, so the same layout can drive hammers, plucked strings, pipes, tines or oscillators. The voice uses air from the lungs to vibrate the vocal folds, and the throat and mouth shape vowels. Electronic instruments generate a waveform that is then filtered and amplified.

lessons.title: Range and Transposing Instruments
body: Written music does not always match what you hear. Transposing instruments sound a different pitch from the note on the page, usually so that players can switch between related instruments without relearning fingerings.

The B-flat clarinet and B-flat trumpet sound a major second below written pitch, so a written C sounds as B-flat. The horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below written. The double bass sounds an octave lower than written, and so does the guitar. The piccolo goes the other way, sounding an octave higher than written. All saxophones share fingerings, with alto and baritone in E-flat and soprano and tenor in B-flat, so a player can move between sizes.

Range is written in scientific pitch notation: the double bass spans about E1 to G4, the cello C2 to C6, the viola C3 to E6, and the violin G3 to A7. The oboe is the orchestra's tuning reference because its pitch is very stable, and everyone tunes to its A.
A trumpeter handed a part with a written C must therefore play a note that the piano would name B-flat.

lessons.title: Musical Form and Reading a Score
body: A full score stacks the staves of every instrument, with bar lines aligned vertically, so you can read down a column and see everything sounding at one moment. Reading it means following the melody, the bass and the way the voices relate.

Form is the large-scale plan. Sonata form has three sections: an exposition that presents themes, a development that explores them, and a recapitulation that returns them. In the first movement of Mozart's Symphony No. 40 in G minor, the second subject arrives in B-flat in the exposition and comes back in G minor in the recapitulation. Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata inverts the usual plan, putting the slow movement first.

A canon is a strict imitation. Pachelbel's Canon is a three-voice canon over a two-bar ground bass repeated twenty-eight times, which makes 56 bars. A fugue begins with one voice stating the subject, and a second voice answers at the dominant. Counterpoint forbids parallel fifths and octaves because they make voices merge into one. Bach's Goldberg Variations has thirty variations built on the same bass line and harmonic plan.
